insight.title: Why we all live inside the same clock
insight.subtitle: The moment time stopped being local and became a machine

sections.text: Before the trains, every village lived by its own sun. High noon in London was several minutes away from high noon in Bristol. People preferred the slow, messy rhythm of their shadows. But as steam engines began to race across the land, these tiny gaps in time became deadly, invisible walls between rushing iron wheels.

To keep engines from colliding, we had to flatten the world. Stations wired their clocks together, forcing hundreds of different "noons" into a single, artificial heartbeat. It was a silent revolution of the wrist. Suddenly, time was no longer a gift from the sky, but a strict schedule dictated by the rhythmic clicking of copper wires.

We traded our unique, solar mornings for a global synchronization that allows us to meet across oceans. This efficiency built the modern world, yet it also disconnected us from our immediate surroundings. We stopped looking up at the light to know the hour. Now, we carry the ghost of those Victorian railway tracks in every digital pocket.
We did not master time; we simply agreed to let it rule us together.

news.title: Jennifer Ihuoma, researcher focused on early biological changes behind brain decline
news.description: Jennifer Ihuoma’s journey into biomedical research began in Imo State, Nigeria, and extends across public health systems and laboratory science in the United States.advertisement Her work focuses on understanding the biological processes that take place in the brain before clinical signs of cognitive decline emerge, with a focus on prevention and early intervention as pathways […]
news.why: New research could help you detect and treat brain decline earlier.

news.title: NASA Artemis II crew captures Earth's brilliant blue beauty as they rocket to moon
news.description: NASA crew takes pictures of home through capsule window; by Friday afternoon, they were more than 110,000 miles from Earth, and are set to pass their destination by Monday
news.why: New mission tech could improve your phone’s GPS and cellular connection.

news.title: Food prices spiked in March as Middle East conflict drove up energy costs, UN says
news.description: Biggest rises were in vegetable oil and sugar prices, which increased by 5% and 7% respectively
news.why: You may pay more for your groceries and fuel this month.

news.title: NC joins lawsuit over Trump’s mail-in ballot order, calling it an unconstitutional power grab
news.description: North Carolina Attorney General Jeff Jackson says he joined the lawsuit to protect North Carolinians who vote by mail, including active-duty military personnel.
news.why: Legal changes could limit how you can cast your next vote.

news.title: Anthropic cuts off the ability to use Claude subscriptions with OpenClaw and third-party AI agents
news.description: To be clear, it will still be possible to use Claude models like Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku to power OpenClaw and similar external agents, but users will now need to opt into a pay-as-you-go or API.
news.why: You may lose access to AI features on some third-party apps.

news.title: Artemis astronauts take photo of Earth en route to Moon
news.description: The four Artemis astronauts have passed the halfway point between Earth and the Moon on the way to their planned lunar flyby, NASA has said.
news.why: Advanced space cameras could help you track weather patterns more accurately.

news.title: 'It beggars belief': UK military reveal locations inside sensitive bases through exercise app
news.description: Some exercise apps use GPS to allow runners to track and share their routes online, but there are concerns Britain's adversaries could exploit the data to identify and target UK military personnel.
news.why: Your fitness tracking apps could accidentally leak your private home address.

news.title: While Ukraine aid runs dry, Trump asks for record-breaking $1.5 trillion in military spending
news.description: The proposed budget calls for a $445 billion (44%) increase in defense funds in 2027 — as U.S. military aid to Ukraine has dropped by 99% under Trump's watch.
news.why: Large military budgets could lead to higher taxes or fewer public services.
